newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: "Worm" brings more good news for NZ Labour.
newsitem.headline: "Worm" brings more good news for NZ Labour.

text.p: New Zealand's opposition Labour Party drew fresh encouragement from an electronic "worm" as party leaders wooed voters on Monday in the final stages of a knife-edge election campaign.

A group of 120 floating voters driving the "worm", a wiggly graph that registers approval or censure of politicians' remarks, rated Labour leader Helen Clark the winner of the campaign's last big televised debate.

Clark, bidding to be New Zealand's first woman prime minister, told viewers she could build a stable left-wing coalition to end six years of conservative government and deliver on promises of better health and education.
She pledged to pick up the phone the day after Saturday's general election and start talking with the leaders of the left-wing Alliance and economic nationalist New Zealand First.

"I'd be very surprised if, in the parties currently represented in opposition, we could not come to a very good agreement on a programme for government for better health, better education and better living standards," she said.
A question mark still hangs over the ability of the three main opposition parties to set aside personal feuds and divisions over economic policy to form a workable coalition.

Opinion polls, however, increasingly suggest the election is theirs for the taking if they can. They jointly average around 52 percent support in the run-up to New Zealand's first election under a German-style proportional system.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger, sharper and more confident than in a previous leaders' debate, defended his government's record of strong economic growth. "We must not go back and tear up the progress we have made," he said.

Despite economic recovery and tax cuts, the government has struggled to fend off attacks over the state of publicly-funded health and education, the issues that matter most to voters. It rates higher than any rival in opinion polls but lacks a strong coalition partner on the right.

The "worm", driven by uncommitted voters using hand-held computers, has generated huge controversy. The conclusion that Clark won the last debate, however, was overwhelmingly shared by political analysts.
Bolger's camp has denounced it as a gimmick. "I think it's a nonsense that this campaign should be dictated to by a worm," the prime minister complained to interviewers.

Financial markets appear broadly comfortable that a Labour-led government would not roll back 12 years of reform that have created one of the world's most open and competitive economies. The main stock market index climbed 1.36 percent on Monday to reach a 2-1/2 year high.
